title: Agent-mediated labeling: workflows and evaluation

slides.title: The conventional labeling workflow
slides.notes: The conventional workflow places two burdens on the human: making a partly tacit conception explicit as a guideline, and repeatedly applying it to varied items. The warning callouts name possible failure modes, not a claim that every conventional dataset is unreliable. This slide motivates the proposed method rather than reporting a comparative experiment.

SLIDE 1. Title: "The conventional labeling workflow"
Subtitle: "The human must articulate the standard and apply it item by item"

One clean left-to-right workflow across the middle, four large illustrated nodes:

GUIDELINE, a written document, caption "Write the rules"

slides.title: Use case 1: a human with an idea
slides.notes: The core unit of human work is a consequential judgment about a rule, group, contrast, exception, or conflict. The agent retrieves cases from the corpus and brings a focused question to the human. It records the answer, updates the rule and identifies affected labels. Information and rules evolve with examples rather than being completed before any labeling occurs. The human retains authority over meaning. An accepted output may be a small reviewed subset or a larger batch accepted under a stated audit policy. Unknown or deferred cases remain visible. High-level judgments can coexist with occasional item checks. Both use cases share the same scaling path. After human approval of the standard, test the same guideline across fixed executor models, refine wording without changing approved meaning, qualify an executor, and apply it to the large unlabeled corpus. Audit batches and route uncertain or conflicting cases back for review. The larger labeled corpus is not assumed to have every item manually reviewed. The three visual rows distinguish dialogue, paired accepted outputs, and execution at scale. The dialogue produces both a structured, adaptive guideline and human-approved, guideline-consistent labeled data. This accepted data may be a small reviewed subset. The two outputs remain aligned as human decisions refine the standard. Adaptive means approved meaning can evolve through human review of new evidence; executor-driven wording changes must preserve approved meaning. Both outputs support executor testing; development examples must remain separate from held-out evaluation cases. The model-expanded corpus is accepted under the stated review or audit policy.

slides.title: Use case 2: an existing labeled corpus
slides.notes: Existing labels are evidence of prior decisions, not unquestioned ground truth. The agent infers candidate rules and constructs issue groups containing supporting items, conflicting cases, contextual differences, alternative explanations and resolution status. A flag does not establish an error. A reviewer can clarify, correct or defer, and need not be the original annotator. An audit without a reviewer may deliver provisional rules and issue groups without certifying an approved standard. Once meaning is accepted, keep the approved semantics fixed while testing wording across independent executor models. Qualification uses unseen cases before large-scale batches and auditing. This scaling stage also follows use case 1. Uniform performance across all models is a research goal, not an established result. The LEFT labeled corpus is starting evidence, not the target collection. Existing labels may reveal patterns but are not automatically gold labels. The human reviewer confirms, revises or defers candidate rules and issue groups. The RIGHT large unlabeled corpus is a distinct target for expansion and supplies new boundary cases. The shared downstream path is structured guideline, cross-model executor testing, and large-scale labeling with audit. Meaning changes require human approval; wording refinement preserves that meaning. The three visual rows distinguish dialogue, paired accepted outputs, and execution at scale. The dialogue produces both a structured, adaptive guideline and human-approved, guideline-consistent labeled data. This accepted data may be a small reviewed subset. The two outputs remain aligned as human decisions refine the standard. Adaptive means approved meaning can evolve through human review of new evidence; executor-driven wording changes must preserve approved meaning. Both outputs support executor testing; development examples must remain separate from held-out evaluation cases. The model-expanded corpus is accepted under the stated review or audit policy.

slides.title: Evaluation 1: human effort and labeling quality
slides.notes: Proposed human study. Compare manual item-level labeling, a human-authored guideline applied by a fixed executor, and agent-mediated guideline formation and labeling. Randomize and counterbalance method order using comparable but separate task sets to reduce carryover. Keep corpus access, task context and downstream executor settings comparable where applicable. Analyze build-from-idea tasks and audit-existing-label tasks separately. Measure total active human time, number and type of judgments, corrections, review effort and subjective workload. Use blinded review of held-out items against task-appropriate adjudicated judgments; for subjective tasks, preserve the intended person's standard and report unresolved disagreement. Select the primary quality metric for the label type before testing. Predefine the acceptable quality difference, and compare effort at comparable quality or under a common budget. In audit tasks, estimate confirmed-issue precision and reviewer effort using independent review. Evaluate natural conflicts separately from deliberately planted label changes. Sampling unflagged cases can help estimate missed issues. Old labels and synthetic perturbations are limited references. Pilot data should guide sample size and power; none is specified yet. No experiment has been run.

slides.title: Evaluation 2: guideline portability and scale
slides.notes: Proposed portability experiment. Hold approved information and rules fixed while comparing initial wording, refinement against a single executor, and refinement against multiple executors. Give refinement methods comparable development data and tuning budgets, and use the same facilitator capability where feasible. Recheck semantic fidelity against the approved standard. Keep development cases, calibration decisions and final evaluation cases separate. Freeze candidate wording and acceptance thresholds before the final test. Test the same guideline in fresh model contexts with fixed weights and allowed inputs only, excluding hidden facilitator conversations. Evaluate inexpensive small, intermediate and strong models, plus previously unseen executor models when feasible. Report quality with uncertainty by model and class, coverage, abstention, cost per accepted item, and human review cost. Select a quality metric suited to the task, such as macro-F1 for appropriate categorical labels, rather than assuming accuracy alone. A useful result raises the weakest required model's quality, limits deterioration of strong models within a predefined tolerance, and lowers total accepted-item cost while meeting coverage requirements. A reduced cross-model gap alone can reflect all models becoming worse. Report guideline-development cost separately and its amortization over corpus volume. If the guideline is revised after test inspection, reserve fresh evaluation cases for the new candidate. Benefits remain hypotheses.

slides.title: Proposed workflow: steps to discuss
slides.notes:
Discussion draft, not a finalized method or an implemented capability claim. Steps 0 and 1 are revisitable: choose an initial task/unit and intended population before reservation; refine substantive meaning through the dialogue. Prepare target items and required context, retain legacy labels with provenance, group related or duplicate items before partitioning, and keep evaluation cases outside development browsing and retrieval. Use case 1 starts with a rough idea; use case 2 starts with old labeled data and an optional guideline. Old labels are evidence, not automatic gold. Human confirms whether to recover a prior standard or establish one for the current purpose.

The agent mediates between human and corpus. It retrieves supporting and contrasting cases, assembles a focused rule or conflict question, records human decisions and applies approved changes to affected items. One human judgment may guide many items. Distinguish directly reviewed labels, model labels inferred under approved rules, and batch acceptance under an explicit audit policy. Unresolved cases do not become negative labels.

The meaning loop changes rules, exceptions or priority only through human decisions. The expression loop preserves approved semantics while comparing wording across independent fixed-weight executor models on development cases. Passing regression cases is evidence of fidelity rather than proof of equivalence. Diagnose semantic issues and return them to human judgment. Adaptive means approved versions evolve; each production batch binds a frozen version.

Before qualification, set quality, coverage, strong-model non-regression and cost criteria. Compare weak and strong executors; a smaller gap alone is insufficient. Do not repeatedly tune wording against the final held-out evaluation. Distinguish model selection from an independent final performance claim. Qualify before scaling, review risky cases and randomly audit apparently consistent cases too. New meaning issues return to step 3 and require a new version and affected-output review.

Open for discussion: what bounded evidence and scope constitute a rule approval or batch acceptance? What random audit coverage, unresolved-risk tolerance and development budget justify stopping? All thresholds remain to be specified. Source: blueprint studio s03-agent-role, s41-task-items-procedure, s42-task-building-procedure, and current haipipe-labeling skills.
